message: Request: Write exactly two English emails introducing MarketingOS to invited early-access testers who already have a test account. They run a small SaaS business and need to write a launch or onboarding email campaign. Explain one concrete supported reason to try the product, then invite them to test one real offer and review the output. Do not assume their present tools, revenue, list size, staffing, email results or urgency. Do not invent prices, testimonials, performance gains or public signup. Make the first action small: sign in, add the real offer material, and request one email. In the second email explain why inspecting source facts and reader feedback is useful. One clear CTA in each email to their existing account. The product is MarketingOS, not the older orqAgent AI agent builder.

Request: Write exactly two English emails introducing MarketingOS to invited early-access testers who already have a test account. They run a small SaaS business and need to write a launch or onboarding email campaign. Explain one concrete supported reason to try the product, then invite them to test one real offer and review the output. Do not assume their present tools, revenue, list size, staffing, email results or urgency. Do not invent prices, testimonials, performance gains or public signup. Make the first action small: sign in, add the real offer material, and request one email. In the second email explain why inspecting source facts and reader feedback is useful. One clear CTA in each email to their existing account. The product is MarketingOS, not the older orqAgent AI agent builder.
Delivered 2 of 2 email(s). Average AI simulation assessment (uncalibrated) 7.0/10.
- Email 1 "Five onboarding emails in an afternoon is a fair comparison": Before anything gets written, your material is compiled into a set of facts the writing is allowed to claim — and then every draft is read by a reader who has never seen the brief, and rewritten where it did not land; that is the part you cannot get from a blank prompt, and it only starts once you put one real offer in. - pull 7/10 after 1 rewrite(s) - and argues from none of the evidence it was assigned
- Email 2 "The quote behind every fact it claims": The notes the pilot asks for — the phrases you would keep or rewrite, the factual errors, the time you spent editing — are measurements only you can take, because you are the one who still checks the facts, the links and the voice before anything leaves. - pull 7/10 after 2 rewrite(s) - and argues from none of the evidence it was assigned
Sequence: Two emails that argue one promise in the right order — earn the run, then make the run's working readable — and both stand alone; the only sequence-level slack is that email 2's reader-report half repeats email 1's claim instead of opening it the way it opens the facts page.}
Email(s) 1, 2: the automatic check did not match the copy to its assigned evidence. Review its claims against the sources; this check can miss paraphrases and does not establish whether a claim is true or invented.
What held the copy back: No price or free-entry terms found - emails cannot name a price, a trial length or a risk reversal; No customer names, quotes or case studies found - the copy can describe the product but cannot prove anyone uses it; No measurable results found - claims stay qualitative, and adjectives convert worse than numbers
What would help most next time: Resolve this simulated next-step obstacle: I would have clicked if this email had told me how long the setup actually takes and what exactly to bring — e.g. 'paste your pricing page and one existing welcome email, about ten minutes, first drafts back in two' — so I could judge whether it fits before the meeting or has to wait for Thursday. Check existing verified material first; surface a supported answer or documentation link appropriate to the CTA. If absent, obtain this specific information. Reader expectations are not product evidence.
